passage: I sat next to Sachin in the Friday review, so I saw it up close. Our regional head put up a chart: the eight cafés that got the new playlist in spring sold more cold drinks than the rest. "Roll it out everywhere," the head said. Sachin tapped his pen twice, the way he does before disagreeing. "Which cafés got it first?" The newest ones, in the big malls. "Then the mall crowds might explain both," he said. "And spring is when cold drinks go up anyway. Can we compare with mall cafés that didn't get the playlist?" The room went quiet. I couldn't tell if he was nervous; his voice stayed level. Two weeks later the comparison came back: almost no difference. I'm Jyoti, and I've copied his pen-tapping ever since.

qa.q: Which cafés got the new playlist first?
qa.a: The newest ones, in the big malls, got it first.

qa.q: What do Sachin's pen-tapping and level voice suggest about his state of mind?
qa.a: They suggest he was uneasy with the quick conclusion and determined to check it, though Jyoti couldn't tell whether he felt nervous.

qa.q: Which of Sachin's questions did the most useful work, and why?
qa.a: Asking to compare with mall cafés that didn't get the playlist, because that comparison group separates the playlist from the crowds and the season.

qa.q: How might the regional head have felt when the comparison came back?
qa.a: The head might have felt a little embarrassed, but also relieved not to roll out a change that made almost no difference.

grounding: Shows an analyst asking whether a third cause or the season explains a sales link and asking for a comparison group before claiming cause.

passage:
Monday. Kavitha burst into the NGO office with a spreadsheet. "The children in our evening reading club improved twice as much as the others this term!" Salma, the programme analyst, read it slowly. "Who chose to join?" "Well, the keen ones. Their parents signed them up." Salma wrote three words on a sticky note: keen, parents, luck.
The next Thursday. Salma found the waiting list: forty children whose parents had also signed up but for whom there had been no space. "They're our comparison," she told Kavitha. "Same keen families, no club yet."
Three weeks later. The new numbers came in. The club children still improved more than the waiting list, but by far less than the first chart had suggested. Kavitha sighed, then smiled. "Smaller, but real." Salma pinned the sticky note above her desk.

qa.q: What did Salma use as a comparison group?
qa.a: She used the waiting list: forty children whose parents had also signed up but for whom there had been no space.

qa.q: Why did Salma write 'keen, parents, luck' on a sticky note?
qa.a: Salma felt cautious rather than excited; she suspected that keen children, involved parents or plain luck could explain the gain, not only the club.

qa.q: Why was the waiting list a smart comparison?
qa.a: Those children came from equally keen families, so any extra gain in the club group is more likely due to the club itself.

qa.q: How did Kavitha's feelings change from Monday to the final numbers?
qa.a: Kavitha went from bursting with excitement to a small sigh, then accepted a smaller but real effect with a smile.

grounding: Shows an analyst asking whether keen families or luck explain a link and finding a comparison group before claiming the club caused the gain.

passage: Samir, sit, you'll like this one. I, Yogesh, was about your age, twenty-four, in my first year at the district agriculture office. My boss dropped a report on my desk: villages with more tractors had bigger harvests. The plan was to send tractors to every village. I was new and scared to speak. But I kept thinking: which villages have tractors? The ones with canal water. Maybe water grows the crops and also makes farmers rich enough to buy tractors. And maybe good harvests bought the tractors, not the other way round. So I asked for two lists: canal villages with few tractors, and dry villages with many. My boss grumbled for a week. The lists showed water did most of the work. The funds went to repairing canals instead. Always ask what else could explain it, beta.

qa.q: What did the report on young Yogesh's desk claim?
qa.a: It claimed that villages with more tractors had bigger harvests.

qa.q: What was young Yogesh feeling when the report arrived, and what kept the doubt alive?
qa.a: Yogesh felt new and scared to speak, but a nagging curiosity about canal water, and about which came first, kept the doubt going.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Asking for canal villages with few tractors and dry villages with many; those comparison lists showed water did most of the work, so the funds went to canals.

qa.q: How might the boss have felt about the request for two more lists?
qa.a: The boss seems to have been irritated by the delay, grumbling for a week, before the lists changed the plan.

grounding: Shows a young analyst asking whether water, reverse direction or coincidence explained a tractors-and-harvests link and comparing villages first.

passage: In the Class 5 corridor, Sahil hopped on one foot, pulling his socks off and on again. "What are you doing?" Bhupen asked. "Inside out. Yesterday I wore them inside out by mistake, and the maths test got cancelled. So today, bye-bye science test." Bhupen pointed at the notice board. "The maths test got cancelled because Rao Ma'am went to a wedding." "But it happened right after the socks!" Sahil said. The science teacher walked in on time, carrying a fat stack of papers. Sahil's shoulders fell. He wrote the test with both socks inside out anyway, just in case. At lunch he told Bhupen, "Maybe the socks only work on Mondays." Bhupen laughed so hard the whole bench shook.

qa.q: Why was the maths test actually cancelled?
qa.a: It got cancelled because Rao Ma'am went to a wedding.

qa.q: Why did Sahil feel so sure the socks had cancelled the test?
qa.a: Sahil felt hopeful and clever, because the cancellation came right after the socks, and something that follows so closely seems caused by it.

qa.q: What could Sahil check before trusting the socks again?
qa.a: He could keep a record of sock days and test days, and look at the real reasons tests change, like the notice on the board.

qa.q: How does Bhupen see the socks idea?
qa.a: Bhupen finds it funny, since the notice board already gave the real reason for the cancellation.

grounding: Shows a child believing inside-out socks cancelled a test because the cancellation came right after.

passage:
Saturday. The fields behind Santosh's house were cracked and grey. His little sister Nirmala watched him stamp and spin in the courtyard, arms up. "It's a rain dance," he panted. "I made it up."
Sunday. Thunder rolled in after lunch, and fat drops hit the tin roof. Santosh ran out shouting, "I did it! Nirmala, I did it!" He told Aai, the neighbour's boys and the man at the ration shop.
The next Friday. The sky stayed empty. Santosh danced twice, once with his eyes shut. Nothing. Aai reminded him that the radio had said on Saturday morning that rain was coming on Sunday. Santosh sat on the step for a long time, then asked, "So the rain was coming anyway?" Nirmala nodded. He still danced whenever it rained, but only for fun.

qa.q: When did the rain come after Santosh's dance?
qa.a: Thunder rolled in on Sunday after lunch, and fat drops hit the tin roof.

qa.q: What was Santosh feeling when the rain came on Sunday, and why did he believe the dance worked?
qa.a: Santosh felt thrilled and proud, because the rain came the day after his dance, so it seemed the dance had caused it.

qa.q: What helped Santosh see what really happened, and how could he test ideas like this again?
qa.a: Aai reminded him of Saturday's radio forecast; he could try the dance on several dry days and see whether rain follows.

qa.q: What might the week have been like for Nirmala?
qa.a: Nirmala probably enjoyed her brother's excitement, then saw his disappointment, and quietly agreed when he worked out the rain was coming anyway.

grounding: Shows a child crediting his dance for rain that simply came after it, and learning about the forecast later.

passage: Yogesh, you think your cold came from yesterday's lemonade? Let your Nana tell you something. When I was nine, in our lane in Indore, I had one cup of mango ice cream at my cousin's birthday. That night I woke up burning with fever. For three whole years I refused ice cream. I was sure it had done it. At every wedding I pushed the bowl away, feeling very wise. Then one summer the school doctor came to our class and asked how many of us had got a fever after ice cream. A few hands. Then she asked how many had got a fever without any ice cream. Nearly every hand. My friend Rafiq whispered, "So the fever was just coming, Tejas." I felt so silly I laughed out loud. Three years of mango, gone for nothing.

qa.q: What did young Tejas eat at the cousin's birthday?
qa.a: Young Tejas had one cup of mango ice cream.

qa.q: Why did young Tejas feel so sure the ice cream caused the fever?
qa.a: He felt frightened and then wise, because the fever came the very night after the ice cream, so it seemed obviously caused by it.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Nana's story, and why did it change his mind?
qa.a: The school doctor asked who had got a fever without ice cream, and nearly every hand went up, showing fevers came anyway.

qa.q: How might Rafiq have seen those three years without ice cream?
qa.a: Rafiq seems to have found it a little funny and kindly pointed out that the fever was just coming anyway.

grounding: Shows a child blaming ice cream for a fever just because the fever came after it.

qa.q: Why does Disha feel sure the tonic cured the cold?

qa.q: What does Farhan suggest before Disha buys more, and why is it sensible?

passage: The week before the prelims, Nirmala bought a red-and-black thread from a stall at the Kolhar fair. She tied it on her wrist and then scored eighty-one in science, her best ever. "It's the thread," she told Vidya on the bus home, tapping it. "I'm never taking it off." Vidya glanced at her friend's notebook, crowded with diagrams. "You also studied every evening at my house for a month. You never did that before." "Lots of people study. Not everyone has this." Vidya didn't argue. In the next test Nirmala wore the thread but skipped the evening sessions for a cousin's wedding. She got fifty-four. Staring at the paper, she turned the thread round and round on her wrist, and slowly said, "Maybe it was the evenings."

qa.q: What score did Nirmala get in science after tying on the thread?
qa.a: She scored eighty-one in science, her best ever.

qa.q: Why did the thread feel responsible for the good mark to Nirmala?
qa.a: Nirmala felt proud and lucky, and the thread arrived just before her best mark, so it seemed to be the cause, while the month of studying felt ordinary.

qa.q: What could Nirmala do to keep her marks up next time?
qa.a: Keep the evening study sessions going, thread or no thread, since the fifty-four came when those sessions stopped.

qa.q: Why might Vidya have chosen not to argue on the bus?
qa.a: Vidya may have sensed that Nirmala was happy and attached to the thread, and that arguing would only make the thread seem more important.

grounding: Shows a teenager crediting a lucky thread for a high score when a month of study came with it.

passage: In Lagos, the French results were pinned to the classroom door, and Chidi pushed through the crowd to find a seventy-eight, up from fifty-two. "It's the app," Chidi told Oskar, holding up the phone. "Ten minutes of flashcards a day for a week. Look at that jump!" Oskar scanned the list. "Everyone jumped. Tunde went up twenty, and he doesn't even have a phone." "Tunde's different." "Madame Okafor said this test was only on the easy chapters." Chidi frowned at the list, then at the phone. The flashcards had felt like magic. "Okay. So I don't know yet if it helped." "Keep using it. See what happens on the hard chapters." Chidi nodded, a little deflated, and set a reminder for seven o'clock.

qa.q: What mark did Chidi get in French?
qa.a: Chidi got a seventy-eight, up from fifty-two.

qa.q: Why did the app feel like the reason for the jump to Chidi?
qa.a: Chidi felt excited and proud, and since the higher mark came right after a week of flashcards, the app seemed like magic.

qa.q: What is a fair way for Chidi to find out whether the app helps?
qa.a: Keep using it and watch the marks on the hard chapters, comparing with classmates who don't use it, like Tunde.

qa.q: How does Oskar see the jump in marks?
qa.a: Oskar notices that everyone's marks jumped because the test covered only the easy chapters, so the app may not explain it.

grounding: Shows a teenager crediting a flashcard app for a better mark when an easier test raised everyone's scores.

passage: You want the story, Ujjwal? Fine. I'm Yash, and last winter I had a cough that wouldn't quit. My aunt heard and started forwarding messages. One said a neighbour's son drank some bitter herb water and was cured the very next morning. Another was a video of a man saying his cough vanished after two days of a leaf paste. Every morning, three or four new forwards: "Try this, beta, it WORKED." Honestly, I was tempted. The timing sounded so neat: drink it, wake up fine. But I kept thinking, how many people drank it and stayed sick? Nobody forwards those. And coughs often ease on their own. So I went to the campus clinic instead. The doctor listened to my chest and checked me properly. I got better. My aunt still thinks it was the leaf paste I never took.

qa.q: Who forwarded the cure messages to Yash?
qa.a: Yash's aunt forwarded the messages.

qa.q: Why did Yash feel tempted by the forwards?
qa.a: Yash felt worn down by the cough and tempted, because the stories had such neat timing, drink it and wake up fine, that the herb seemed to work.

qa.q: What choice did Yash make, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Yash went to the campus clinic, where a doctor checked properly, instead of trusting stories that never mention the people who stayed sick.

qa.q: How does the aunt probably see Yash's recovery?
qa.a: The aunt probably feels caring and still sure the remedies work, even crediting a leaf paste Yash never took.

grounding: Shows a student receiving forwarded cure stories whose neat timing is tempting, while noticing natural recovery and going to a doctor.

passage:
Tuesday. Lavanya twisted her ankle in the inter-hostel football match. At the college clinic, the doctor strapped it, told her to rest it, and booked her in for physiotherapy.
Friday. The hostel group pinged all evening. A forward claimed a girl in Mysuru rubbed a special herbal oil on a sprain and walked the very next day. Ganga, her roommate, bought a bottle from the market and set it on Lavanya's desk. "Just try it. It worked for that girl overnight." Lavanya rubbed a little on, mostly to make Ganga happy, and felt the pull of the story anyway.
The following Thursday. The ankle was much better. "The oil!" Ganga cried. Lavanya looked at the calendar. She had rested it and done the physio exercises every day. "Or it was just healing, Ganga. That's what the physio said would happen." She kept up the physio and left the oil on the shelf.

qa.q: Where did Lavanya twist her ankle?
qa.a: She twisted it in the inter-hostel football match.

qa.q: What was Lavanya feeling on Friday when the oil appeared?
qa.a: Lavanya felt the pull of the story and wanted to make Ganga happy, while still unsure the oil did anything.

qa.q: What did Lavanya do on Thursday that showed good thinking?
qa.a: She checked the calendar, remembered the rest and the daily physio exercises, and kept following the physio instead of crediting the oil.

qa.q: How does Ganga see the ankle getting better?
qa.a: Ganga, who clearly cares about Lavanya, sees the recovery as proof the oil worked, because it came after the oil.

grounding: Shows a student receiving a forwarded overnight-cure story and a push to try an oil, then noticing the ankle was healing with rest and physio.

passage: Jasleen, you keep showing me these forwards about miracle leaves, so let your Jaya bua tell you something. When I was twenty, at college in Amritsar, I had a fever that went on and on. There were no phones then, but news still travelled: every neighbour at our door had a story. "Mrs Gill's nephew took this root powder and was up the next morning!" My mother, frightened, wanted to try every one. I wanted to believe too; the stories were so neat. But my professor had once said something I never forgot: "You only hear about the ones who got up the next morning." So I asked Mother to take me back to Dr Bhatia, who ran proper tests and treated me. I took one spoon of the powder, only to please Mother. It took time, but I recovered. Those neighbours still say it was the root powder.

qa.q: What did the neighbours say Mrs Gill's nephew took?
qa.a: Mrs Gill's nephew took a root powder and was up the next morning.

qa.q: Why did the neighbours' stories tempt young Jaya?
qa.a: Jaya was ill, tired and hopeful, and the stories were so neat, taken today and well tomorrow, that the timing felt like proof.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Jaya's story?
qa.a: Remembering the professor's words that you only hear about the ones who got up the next morning, and asking Mother to go back to Dr Bhatia for proper tests and treatment.

qa.q: How did Jaya's mother experience the neighbours' stories?
qa.a: Her mother was frightened and wanted to try every remedy, because each story offered hope for her sick daughter.

grounding: Shows a young woman receiving story after story of overnight cures and choosing a doctor over timing that ignored natural recovery.

passage: In the school staffroom, Nilesh was waving a printout. "Since I started the five-minute brain-gym claps before class, my Class 7 scores have gone up. We should do it school-wide." Hemant, who taught maths next door, read the numbers. "Up from the first test, which was the hardest of the year," he said. "What would your scores have done without the claps?" Nilesh blinked. "Gone up anyway, maybe?" "Maybe. Let's find out. You do the claps in 7A, I'll skip them in 7B. Same tests, whole term." Nilesh agreed, grinning. By March the two sections were almost level. Nilesh kept the claps because the children liked them, and quietly dropped the plan to make them compulsory for the whole school.

qa.q: Which section did Hemant say would skip the claps?
qa.a: Hemant said he would skip them in 7B.

qa.q: Why did Hemant feel doubtful about the rise in scores?
qa.a: Hemant felt cautious because the first test was the hardest of the year, so the scores might have risen anyway without the claps.

qa.q: Why was the 7A and 7B plan a good test?
qa.a: With the same tests over a whole term and only one section doing the claps, it shows what happens without them, instead of just before and after.

qa.q: How might Nilesh have felt when the two sections came out almost level?
qa.a: Nilesh may have felt a little disappointed, but kept the claps for the children's enjoyment and let go of making them compulsory.

grounding: Shows a teacher asking what would have happened without a change and setting up a comparison between sections before believing it.

passage:
Hi Asif,
I've been thinking about our call on Sunday. You said the herbal powder from the gym fixed your headaches, since they stopped the week you started it. I'm really glad they've stopped. 🙂 But that was also the week your exams ended and you started sleeping properly again, remember? Either of those could be it, or the headaches might have eased on their own.
I'm not saying the powder did nothing. I'm saying we can't tell from one week. And headaches that keep coming back deserve a proper doctor's visit, not just a powder a gym trainer suggested. Would you book one? I'll come with you if you like, the way you came with me for my wrist last year.
If the doctor says it's all fine, drink your powder in peace.
Love,
Uma

qa.q: When did Asif say the headaches stopped?
qa.a: Asif said they stopped the week the powder was started.

qa.q: What is Uma feeling while writing the email?
qa.a: Uma feels glad that the headaches have eased, but concerned that one week can't show the powder was the cause.

qa.q: What does Uma suggest, and why is it the wise step?
qa.a: Uma suggests booking a proper doctor's visit, because headaches that keep coming back need a real check, and a doctor can say what actually helps.

qa.q: How might Asif feel reading the email?
qa.a: Asif might feel a bit defensive about the powder at first, but supported by the offer to come along.

grounding: Shows someone asking what would have happened without a remedy, pointing to other changes and urging a doctor for a recurring health problem.

passage: So, Jahnavi, you asked on your show how I decide what to sell. Here's a real example. I'm Elizabeth, and I run a small plant nursery in Kochi. Last monsoon a supplier swore by his new compost: "Put it in, and your chilli seedlings shoot up in a week." And they did! The first tray I tried grew like crazy. Everyone wanted me to stock it. But I kept asking: would they have shot up anyway? It was monsoon, warm and wet; everything grows. So I did it properly: two trays side by side, same seeds, same sun, one with the new compost and one without. Then I repeated it twice more. The compost trays came out a little taller, but only a little. I stocked it in the end, but I tell customers the honest version.

qa.q: Where does Elizabeth run the plant nursery?
qa.a: Elizabeth runs it in Kochi.

qa.q: Why did Elizabeth stay wary even after the first tray grew so well?
qa.a: Elizabeth felt curious but wary, because monsoon weather makes everything grow, so the fast growth might have happened without the compost.

qa.q: Which part of Elizabeth's testing made the result trustworthy?
qa.a: Growing two trays side by side with only the compost different, and repeating it twice more, showed what happened without it.

qa.q: How might the supplier feel about the honest version Elizabeth tells customers?
qa.a: The supplier might feel frustrated that the big promise is toned down, though the compost still gets stocked.

grounding: Shows someone asking what would have happened without a change and using side-by-side, repeated trials before believing it.

passage: Last month I had my birthday, and I planned everything myself. I'm Pankaj, and I love karela sabzi more than anything, so I asked Mummy to make a big pot for my friends. I also chose my favourite game, carrom, for the whole afternoon, and my favourite cartoon film for after. I thought everyone loves those things. When the plates came out, Usha made a face and pushed the karela to one side. Two boys wanted to play cricket instead of carrom, and nobody laughed at the film's jokes. My ears went hot and I went to the balcony. Usha came out and said, "Your party is nice. We just like different things." Next year I'm going to ask everyone first. But I'm still making karela.

qa.q: What food did Pankaj ask Mummy to make for the party?
qa.a: Pankaj asked for a big pot of karela sabzi.

qa.q: Why did Pankaj feel hurt when the friends didn't enjoy the party?
qa.a: Pankaj felt hurt and embarrassed, because karela, carrom and the film seemed like things everyone loves, so the friends' faces came as a shock.

qa.q: What could Pankaj try for next year's party?
qa.a: Ask each friend what they like to eat and play first, and maybe mix one of Pankaj's favourites with one of theirs.

qa.q: How might Usha have felt at the party?
qa.a: Usha probably didn't enjoy the karela but still cared about Pankaj, and so came out to the balcony to say the party was nice.

grounding: Shows a child assuming friends share the same favourite food, game and film, and feeling hurt when they differ.

passage:
Class 3 teacher's note, Friday.
We voted today on where to go for the class trip. Before I even handed out the slips, Harsha stood up: "Everybody wants the planetarium! It's the best." Harsha said it the way you say the sky is blue. When I read the slips aloud, most said the zoo and a few said the water park. Only Harsha and Divyansh chose the planetarium. Harsha's face crumpled. "But why? Stars are the best thing." Divyansh leaned over and whispered, "I like stars too." I asked the class to each say one thing they liked about their choice. Harsha listened, arms folded, then said quietly, "Some people like animals more, I guess." I've promised Harsha and Divyansh a planetarium corner in the classroom next month.

qa.q: Which place got the most votes for the class trip?
qa.a: The zoo got the most votes.

qa.q: What does Harsha's crumpled face suggest about how Harsha felt?
qa.a: It suggests Harsha felt shocked and hurt, having been sure that everyone loved stars as much as Harsha does.

qa.q: How did the teacher help Harsha, and what else could help?
qa.a: The teacher had each child say what they liked about their choice, so Harsha heard real reasons; asking friends before announcing what everyone wants would also help.

qa.q: What was it like for Divyansh when the votes were read out?
qa.a: Divyansh was in the small group who chose the planetarium too, and whispered support, perhaps feeling a little left out as well.

grounding: Shows a child sure that everyone shares a favourite outing and being surprised and hurt by the class vote.

passage:
Sunday night
I made Sahil watch my favourite film today, the one with the robot dog. I've seen it eleven times. I was SO sure he'd love it, because everyone loves it, obviously. I even asked Ammi to make popcorn with extra butter, because that's how everybody likes it.
Sahil didn't laugh at the parts where I laugh. At the best bit, where the dog comes back, he was looking at his hands. After, he said, "It's okay. Bit babyish." BABYISH. My stomach dropped. Then he said his favourite is the scary ghost one, which I hate!! How can someone not like the robot dog?
Ammi said maybe next time Sahil picks the film. I said fine. But I am skipping the ghost parts.
Vaibhav

qa.q: How many times has Vaibhav seen the robot dog film?
qa.a: Vaibhav has seen it eleven times.

qa.q: Why did Vaibhav feel so shocked when Sahil called the film babyish?
qa.a: Vaibhav felt hurt and stunned, because loving the robot dog film seemed like something everyone shares, so a friend not liking it felt impossible.

qa.q: What small step would help the next film night go better?
qa.a: Taking turns to choose, as Ammi suggested, or asking Sahil what films he likes before planning.

qa.q: What might Sahil have felt during the film?
qa.a: Sahil seemed bored and perhaps awkward, looking at his hands during the best bit and trying to be polite with 'It's okay'.

grounding: Shows a child assuming a friend loves the same film and snack, and feeling hurt on finding the friend's tastes differ.

passage: Last term I made a fool of myself over Mr Kulkarni, our new physics teacher. I'm Akash, and I found him boring: he wrote everything on the board and never told jokes. I was sure the whole of 10C felt the same, because my two closest friends did. So at lunch, in front of eight people, I said loudly, "Kulkarni is the worst teacher this school has ever hired." I waited for laughs. Instead Disha put down her roti and said he was the first teacher who had ever made current electricity make sense to her. Three others nodded. My face burned and I snapped that they were just sucking up. Walking home, I realised I had only ever asked two people. That's not a whole class.

qa.q: What did Disha say about Mr Kulkarni?
qa.a: Disha said he was the first teacher who had ever made current electricity make sense to her.

qa.q: Why did Akash snap at the others when they disagreed?
qa.a: Akash felt embarrassed and attacked, having been so sure the whole class agreed that a different view felt like a personal challenge.

qa.q: What could Akash do before sharing a strong opinion with a group?
qa.a: Akash could ask a few people what they think first, and remember that two close friends aren't the whole class.

qa.q: How might Disha have felt when Mr Kulkarni was called the worst teacher?
qa.a: Disha probably felt uncomfortable, but brave enough to defend a teacher who had helped her understand physics.

grounding: Shows a teenager assuming the whole class shares an opinion of a teacher, saying it bluntly, then feeling attacked when others disagree.

passage:
Drama club supervisor's note, 9 February.
During the break Abhinav put on a clip of a pop singer everyone's been talking about and started mimicking her dance, calling it "the cringiest thing on earth, right, guys?" He clearly expected the room to laugh with him. Swati said, "I actually love her songs," and two others agreed. Abhinav went red. "You're joking. Nobody likes that." When they kept disagreeing, he packed his bag and said everyone was ganging up on him. I asked him to stay back. We talked about how many people he had actually asked before deciding that everyone agreed. He admitted it was his cousin and one friend. I suggested he try asking "what do you think?" before announcing. He rolled his eyes, but he nodded.

qa.q: What did Abhinav call the pop singer's dance?
qa.a: He called it 'the cringiest thing on earth'.

qa.q: Why did Abhinav feel ganged up on?

passage:
Note to myself after Sunday lunch. Sharmila.
Santosh came home from his Bengaluru college for the holiday, and at lunch the talk turned to the plan to build a bus depot on the old lake bed. Santosh laughed and said, "Obviously no one supports that. It's destroying a lake." His Chacha said he supported it: the depot would bring jobs and cut his commute. My husband agreed. Santosh looked at them as if they had grown horns. "Seriously? Everyone I know is against it." He meant his hostel and his environment club, I think. He went quiet, then argued too sharply, and left the table before the kheer. I found him on the terrace later and asked how many people he knew who ride the bus to work. None, he said. I told him that's worth thinking about, and that his view is still worth arguing for, calmly.

qa.q: What was planned for the old lake bed?
qa.a: A bus depot was planned for the old lake bed.

qa.q: Why was Santosh so shocked when Chacha supported the depot?
qa.a: Santosh felt stunned and a little offended, because everyone he talks to at the hostel and the environment club is against it, so his view seemed universal.

qa.q: What did Sharmila's question on the terrace help Santosh see, and what could he do next?
qa.a: It showed that he knows nobody who rides the bus to work; next he could ask Chacha why he supports the depot and argue his own view calmly.

qa.q: How might Chacha have seen Santosh's reaction at lunch?
qa.a: Chacha may have felt dismissed, since jobs and a shorter commute were real reasons that Santosh treated as unthinkable.

grounding: Shows a young adult whose circle all agree assuming his view is universal and being shocked by relatives' different views at a family lunch.

passage:
Cousin Rupal's wedding, day 2, very late.
Had the weirdest conversation at the sangeet. I said to Keerthana, half joking, "Thank god our generation is done with arranged marriages, right?" I thought that was just a fact. Everyone in my college group says it. Keerthana looked at me for a long second and said her parents are finding someone for her and she's actually glad about it. That she trusts them, and likes that it's not all on her. Then Mausi joined in, and two cousins, and suddenly I was the odd one out at my own family's wedding. My ears went hot. I argued too much. I think I actually said "that's backwards", which, ugh.
Here's the thing I keep turning over: I don't know a single person who thinks like Keerthana. Or I didn't, until tonight.
Nitin

qa.a: At the sangeet, on day 2 of cousin Rupal's wedding.

qa.q: Why did Keerthana's answer leave Nitin so shaken?
qa.a: Nitin felt shocked and embarrassed, because everyone in Nitin's college group agrees, so that view had seemed like a simple fact.

qa.q: What could Nitin do the next time a family conversation turns to opinions like this?
qa.a: Ask people what they think and why before stating something as obvious, and listen without calling it backwards.

qa.q: How might Keerthana have felt when Nitin said 'that's backwards'?
qa.a: Keerthana may have felt judged and hurt, since she trusts her parents and is glad about her choice.

grounding: Shows a young adult whose friends all agree assuming the view is universal and being shocked by relatives' different views at a family wedding.

passage: The whole Patil family sat on mats in the courtyard in Shirur after the harvest puja, plates of puran poli going round. Uday, home from his agriculture college in Pune, said it casually: "Everyone knows chemical sprays have to go. Organic is the only way now." He reached for another poli. Nobody agreed. Vijay kaka put down his plate. "Everyone? Last year pests took half of Shinde's crop. Without spray I could lose my whole season." Two cousins nodded. Aaji said she had tried organic once and the yield fell. Uday's mouth opened and shut. At college, in his group, he had never heard anyone say otherwise. He spent the evening walking the field edge with Vijay kaka, asking questions for once instead of answering them.

qa.q: What did Vijay kaka say happened to Shinde's crop last year?
qa.a: Pests took half of Shinde's crop.

qa.q: Why was Uday so startled when nobody agreed?
qa.a: Uday felt stunned and a little lost, because everyone in his college group shares the view, so he had believed it was what everyone knows.

qa.q: What did Uday do in the evening, and why was it a good step?
qa.a: He walked the field edge with Vijay kaka asking questions, which let him hear the reasons of someone whose season depends on the choice.

qa.q: How does Vijay kaka see Uday's 'everyone knows'?
qa.a: Vijay kaka hears it as coming from someone who doesn't risk losing a whole season, so it sounds unfair to farmers fighting pests.

grounding: Shows a young man from a like-minded college group assuming his view is universal and being shocked by family disagreement at a harvest meal.

passage:
Wednesday
Almost booked karaoke for the team outing today. I love karaoke, my friends love karaoke, and I was ready to call it the obvious choice. Then I remembered last year's picnic, which I planned for "everyone", and half the team didn't come. So I ran a quick anonymous poll instead. Karaoke came fourth! First was a cooking class, which I'd never have guessed. That surprise bugged me, in a good way.
I went to Deepika's desk, since she's the quietest in the team and nothing like me, and asked what she'd actually enjoy. She said most of the older staff dread singing in public, and a few can't stay late because of their kids. I had never thought of that once.
Cooking class it is, on a Saturday morning. Note to self: when I'm sure, ask.
Mahima

qa.a: A cooking class came first.

qa.q: How did Mahima feel about the poll result, and why does that matter?
qa.a: Mahima felt surprised and a little bugged, in a good way; treating that surprise as a sign of not knowing the team led to asking Deepika.

qa.a: Running an anonymous poll and then asking Deepika, someone quite unlike Mahima, brought out the dread of singing and the need for a morning slot.

passage: Vandana had driven the library van into Sangole every Thursday for a month, the shelves full of the English novels she had loved at college. Almost nobody borrowed them. Her first thought was that the town didn't read. Then she stopped herself: that was a guess, and she'd been wrong before. So on the fifth Thursday she parked by the bangle shop and simply asked. Ritu, who ran the shop and had left school at fourteen, laughed. "Who has time for fat books? Give us short stories in Marathi. And something on sewing patterns." A group of college boys asked for exam guides. An old man wanted newspapers read aloud. Vandana wrote it all in a notebook, a little stung and very curious. The next month the van carried half its shelves in Marathi, and a queue formed before she had parked.

qa.q: Where did Vandana park on the fifth Thursday?
qa.a: She parked by the bangle shop.

qa.q: What was Vandana feeling as she wrote down the requests?
qa.a: Vandana felt a little stung but very curious, treating the surprise as information about what people actually want.

qa.q: Which choice turned the library van around?
qa.a: Dropping the guess that the town didn't read and asking people like Ritu directly, then changing the shelves to match.

qa.a: Ritu would likely feel listened to, seeing Marathi stories on the shelves after being asked, rather than books chosen for someone else.

passage:
Monday. Bhupen, eleven, had promised Aai he'd teach his little brother Omkar to tie shoelaces before school started. "Loop, wrap, pull. Done." He did it in two seconds. Omkar stared at the tangle in his own fingers. "Again!" Bhupen did it faster. Omkar's lip wobbled. "You're not even trying!" Bhupen shouted, and stomped off.
Wednesday. Bhupen watched Aai teach Omkar a song, one line at a time, waiting after each. He thought about his own shoelaces. When had he learned? He couldn't remember not knowing.
Saturday. Bhupen sat on the step with Omkar and one big shoe. "First, make a bunny ear. Just one. Show me." He waited. "Now the other lace goes round the ear like a scarf." It took twenty minutes and three restarts. When the bow held, Omkar shrieked. Bhupen grinned even wider than his brother.

qa.q: What had Bhupen promised Aai?
qa.a: He had promised to teach his little brother Omkar to tie shoelaces before school started.

qa.q: Why did Bhupen get so frustrated on Monday?
qa.a: Bhupen felt impatient and angry, because tying laces seemed so obvious to him that he couldn't see how many steps Omkar was missing.

qa.q: What changed in Bhupen's teaching on Saturday, and why did it work?
qa.a: He broke it into one small step at a time, a bunny ear first, and waited for Omkar to show him, just as Aai did with the song.

qa.q: What was Monday like for Omkar?
qa.a: Omkar felt lost and close to tears, watching the laces flash by in two seconds and then being shouted at.

grounding: Shows an older child skipping steps that seem obvious to him while teaching his little brother, then learning to slow down.

passage: Vidya, you're cross that your little brother can't learn long division from you? Sit. Your Dada Chetan was just the same. When I was ten, I tried to teach my sister Kamla to ride my old cycle in the lane behind the mill. I'd been riding for years. I said, "Just pedal and balance, it's easy!" and let go. She fell. I said it again, louder, and let go again. She fell again and scraped her knee. I got so angry I threw my cap on the ground. My father had watched all of this, and he asked me, "Chetan, do you remember your first day?" I didn't. I couldn't remember ever not knowing. So he said, "Then start where she is." Next morning I held the seat and ran beside her, one pedal at a time. By Sunday she was racing me.

qa.a: His father asking whether he remembered his first day and telling him to start where she is; next morning Chetan held the seat and went one pedal at a time.

qa.a: Kamla was probably scared and sore, being let go again and again and scraping her knee while her brother shouted.

passage: The wedding band in the next building had started, drums thumping through the window, and Zaid's subtraction homework was due in the morning. Ammi was at work till nine.
